c.text: Chapter 6 – Running a Meeting People Want to
Attend
Volunteers do not resent work; they resent wasted evenings
A volunteer will give you a Saturday morning cheerfully.
What they will not give you, twice, is ninety minutes on a weeknight that achieved nothing they could name on the drive home.

Bad meetings are one of the most common reasons good people go cold on a ministry, and new leaders create them without realising, usually with the best intentions. We call everyone together because togetherness feels like leadership. Then we fill the time, because we called it.

Ask whether people can explain why the meeting mattered and what happens next. Some meetings are for decisions; others are for learning, prayer or care. Each needs a clear purpose rather than an evening filled by habit.
The Jerusalem council was a well-run meeting
Acts 15 is worth reading purely as a case study in process.
The question was whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses – a dispute serious enough to threaten the unity of the whole church.
Watch the structure.

The apostles and elders met specifically to consider this question (v. 6). There was much discussion – real, open debate. Then Peter spoke from his own experience with Cornelius. Then Barnabas and Paul reported what God had done among the Gentiles, and the assembly listened in silence. Then James summarised, tied it to Scripture, and proposed a judgement (v. 19).

And then the part everyone forgets: they wrote it down and sent it out. Verses 22-31 describe choosing men to carry a letter to Antioch, explaining the decision. When the letter was read, the church was glad for its encouragement.
One clear question.
Evidence from people who had actually been there. Genuine debate. A stated decision. A written communication to those affected.
Most church meetings fail on the first item and the last two.
Acts 6, again, but for the process
We looked at Acts 6 in Chapter 2 to consider how the apostles shared responsibility. Now look at how the problem was brought to the community and addressed.
A complaint arises.

The Twelve gather the disciples, state the problem plainly, propose a solution, define the criteria for the seven, and ask the group to choose them. The group is pleased with the proposal, names seven men, and the apostles pray and lay hands on them.

The passage gives a concise account of a problem, a proposal and an appointment. Six verses do not tell us how many hours the process took. The useful lesson is clarity of responsibility and follow- through, not speed at any cost.
Preparation helps a meeting move forward, while leaving room to test a proposal and hear the people affected.
Do the thinking before, not during

Proverbs 15:22 says plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed. That is an argument for consulting people – it is not an argument for doing your thinking out loud in a room of twelve.
The single biggest improvement you can make is this: arrive with a proposal, not a blank page.
Write down, before the meeting, what you think should happen and why. Then present it as a proposal you genuinely want tested. “Here’s what I’m thinking, and here’s why. Tell me what I’ve got wrong.”

People engage far better with something concrete than with an open question. “What should we do about the welcome team?” produces silence or wandering. “I think we should move to two teams alternating fortnightly – what’s wrong with that?” produces useful pushback in thirty seconds.
This is not pre-deciding. If nobody can change your mind, you did not need the meeting.
Nehemiah’s short, effective meeting
Nehemiah 2:17-18 is a two-verse meeting and it moved a city.

Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, has arrived in Jerusalem and inspected the ruined walls quietly by night. Then he gathers the priests, nobles, officials and the rest and says three things: you see the trouble we are in – Jerusalem lies in ruins and its gates are burned; come, let us rebuild the wall, so we will no longer be in disgrace; and then he tells them how God’s hand had been on him and what the king had said.
Their answer in verse 18: let us start rebuilding.
The problem, named honestly. The action, stated clearly. The evidence that God is in it. That is the whole thing.
Notice he had walked the walls himself first.
He did not call the meeting to find out what the situation was. He came knowing.
Order is a spiritual concern

1 Corinthians 14 is Paul dealing with Corinthian gatherings that had become genuinely chaotic – people speaking in tongues over each other, prophecies interrupting prophecies. In verse 33 he gives his reason for insisting on structure: God is not a God of disorder but of peace. He closes the section in verse 40 by saying everything should be done in a fitting and orderly way.
Order is not the enemy of the Spirit.
Paul treats disorder as the thing that blocks people from being built up.

Applied to your leadership meeting, that means starting on time and finishing on time is a pastoral act, not bureaucracy. Finishing when you said you would tells a mother of three that you respect her babysitter arrangement. It is one of the clearest ways you communicate that you value people.
The format
One page, sent at least two days ahead.
Before the meeting
State the purpose in one sentence.
Give each item a time allowance and label it decide, discuss or inform.
Send accessible reading in advance.
Move routine information to a message where that will work for the team.
During
Start on time.
Pray meaningfully.
Address the most demanding item while people are fresh.
Invite different perspectives.
Record each decision, its owner and its deadline. If an item needs more time, agree a follow-up
rather than assuming everyone can stay.
After
Send a brief record of decisions, owners and deadlines, with any context people need. Keep

confidential matters in the appropriate restricted record. Check progress before the next meeting. That last habit – checking in between meetings – is what stops your next meeting from becoming a review of everything that didn’t happen.
Two people you will have to manage

The one who dominates. Usually well-meaning and often the most experienced person there. Handle it structurally rather than personally: “I’d like to hear from someone who hasn’t spoken yet.” If it persists, have a private conversation, thank them for their contribution, and ask for their help in drawing out the quieter members. Giving them that job usually solves it.

The one who rarely speaks. They may be reflecting, uncertain, excluded or more comfortable contributing in writing. Invite their view without putting them on the spot: “Grace, would you like to add anything, now or after the meeting?” Leave time for a reply.
Silence may mean someone is thinking.
It may also signal uncertainty or discomfort. Make room for different ways to contribute.
How often
Meet as often as the work and the people need.
Decisions, coordination, prayer, training and care can all justify meeting; habit alone is a poor reason.

If your team meets monthly out of habit and half the meetings have nothing to decide, move to quarterly for planning and handle the rest by message. Then use the time you have freed for what your volunteers actually want more of: someone taking an interest in them personally.
